entries.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
entries.summary: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attentionAmerican author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery
entries.content:
American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch.

Time passes most visibly in Suzanna’s grandmother’s body, the passage towards death harder to deny than the passage towards adulthood. The grandmother, herself a sometime communist with vivid memories of a trip to Russia as a young mother, lives surrounded by friends who are similarly jaded – war-weary Jewish radical thinkers in old age, looking back together on children mostly estranged, dead or far away; husbands who in various ways did not stay the course; wars and regimes more or less survived. Whatever care they receive comes from each other and rarely with good grace. The liveliest conversations – often darkly funny – are about what, if anything, daughters owe to not-good-enough mothers.

Perhaps surprisingly, this isn’t a question that preoccupies Suzanna, who has difficulty acknowledging her own agency. Practically competent as her situation requires her to be, she does not want to ascend the ladder of secondary education or break free from a mother who has no freedom. In some ways, the novel’s tight spatial and temporal circles reminded me of Solvej Balle’s On the Calculation of Volume, in which the same day replays itself for the same people in the same place. Suzanna, whose origin story is abandonment, whose estrangement from her mother runs wide and deep, is in many ways arrested, willing immobility in a small world whose narrowness is no protection from time.

This is, broadly, realist fiction. The material of low-budget, low-energy domesticity is vivid: smelly bedding, mucky floors, stale food. Avoiding sensationalism, Clark writes more about the low-key, cumulative humiliations and discomforts of incarceration than the horror, which is more effective for its shadowiness. A woman newly released from months of strip-lit solitary confinement keeps asking “what time is this”: the worst punishment seems to be the physical manifestation of the timelessness Suzanna craves.

Almost all the physical journeys in The Hill are between the apartment and the prison, mostly by train. The train is another enclosed, shared space, the time on it both liminal and definitive. This feels like a closed-room novel, but it isn’t, or not much more than most novels are. We move from one confinement to another, and back.

It took me a few chapters to trust that the novel was teaching me how to read it. There is much conversation, or at least many interweaving monologues from hard-bitten old women, many of whom speak elliptically, leaving Suzanna and the reader to work out the relevance or significance of half-anecdotes from decades gone by. No one goes anywhere or does anything new, and a lot of the talk is rambling. But it coalesces round incidents and themes, and moments of sharp comedy emerge, as when the grandmother remembers her own mother. “There was nothing like this ridiculously elegant woman weeping into a handkerchief to make life in Stalin’s starving land seem both manageable and promising.” (Not spoiler: wrong.)

The wildness, the light in the cracks, comes from animals that verge on the magical: semi-feral cats enacting a child’s repressed rage, guide dogs in training being fiercely loved in prison and, finally, magnificently, a parrot that can’t fly pacing the aisle of an aeroplane beside a mother in shackles. Read this novel playfully, slowly, with an open mind. It rewards attention.

entries.title: Hannah Lillith Assadi wins US National book award for ‘visionary’ novel Paradiso 17
entries.summary: Assadi’s third novel was inspired by the story of her late father, a Palestinian who escaped the Nakba as a child in 1948Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palesti
entries.content:
Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.

Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.

In a tearful speech, Assadi said, “What a beautiful story this has been, from its origins at my father’s deathbed until now, ending here and accepting this award. And so full of pain.

“In the course of its writing, I have experienced deep personal grief and unimaginable collective grief. I have watched cancer ravage my father’s body and genocide ravage his people and their children. And perhaps this is the Palestinian story on this earth. So beautiful. So painful.”

The judges praised Assadi’s “elegant lyricism” and “ambitious bending of time and space” and called the novel “a visionary, finely wrought portrait of rupture and endurance”.

Assadi won the $10,000 prize against Edwidge Danticat’s Dèy, Julián Delgado Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You, Valeria Luiselli’s Beginning Middle End and Morgan Thomas’ Mad Eden.

Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy won the $10,000 nonfiction prize for his debut Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, about his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy was unable to attend the ceremony after being denied a visa to the US, so his prize was collected by his editor Helen Thomaides, who read out his speech.

ElGendy said he had dreamed of turning his experience into a memoir as it gave him distance from the physical abuse he endured, and revealed he had practised award acceptance speeches under his duvet in prison.

“Today that dream should have come full circle but, like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable,” ElGendy wrote.

The New York Times speculated earlier this month that ElGendy was not even eligible for the award as he did not meet its citizenship or residency requirements after fleeing the US due to Ice deportations, but the National Book Foundation, which administers the National book Awards, disputed this and said it did not “have any concerns regarding the eligibility of his title”.

Samar Yazbek of Syria, a finalist for the books in translation category, was also denied a visa, with the National Book Foundation describing both decisions as “unjust”.

The state department declined to comment on any specific cases, but issued a statement to Associated Press saying that “the Trump Administration continues to put America and its interests first by fully enforcing US immigration laws and ensuring lawful travel through our visa process. As Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio said, ‘a visa is a privilege, not a right’.”

Publishers submitted 1,912 books to the National book awards this year, with the winners judged by panels of authors, editors, booksellers and others in the literary community.

Brenda Hillman won the $10,000 poetry category for Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation, praised as “a rigorously unsentimental portrait of the stillness … of the poet’s childhood home after her mother’s death”.

David Leviathan and Gabriel Duckels won the $10,000 young people’s literature category for The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America.

Indian-British author Salman Rushdie was presented with a medal for “distinguished contribution to American letters”, while paediatrician and author Perri Klass was honoured for “outstanding service to the American literary community”.

Rushdie recalled being welcomed into the US literary scene after spending years under police protection in London after the fatwa over The Satanic Verses, and used his speech to thank the late Ursula K Le Guin for liking his first novel. “She was just about the only one who did! And it meant everything to me,” he said, to laughs.

“All I want to say is that it has been quite a ride, from over there to over here,” he added. “And to ride into this town and end up in this saloon, with these companions, is a hell of a thing.”

Actor and author Kyle MacLachlan hosted the ceremony, held at Cipriani Wall Street, while singer Michelle Zauner, author of the bestselling memoir Crying in H Mart, performed onstage.

entries.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – an intimate meditation on family and memory
entries.summary: The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world warWhen Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. entries.content:
When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.”

Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime.

He learns how his father had been sent away as a boy to be adopted by a priest and his family, but their plans changed and he was returned to his parents. In adulthood, his plans to become a priest were thwarted when he was drafted to fight in the second world war, during which he witnessed untold horror. In tracing the story of his father, and the multiple ways he was abandoned, Murakami unearths deeper truths about family, memory and human vulnerability.

Available from Vintage digital, 1hr 17min

Further listening

Look What You Made Me Do

John Lanchester, WF Howes, 9hr 4min

This black comedy by the Capital author revolves around a married couple who share a private language. When they find their life and language replicated on a TV show; suspicion lands on a young screen­writer. Read by Louise Brealey and Genevieve Gaunt.

Lifeboat at the End of the World

Dominic Gregory, William Collins, 8hr 29min

Gregory, part of a crew of lifeboat volunteers in Dungeness, Kent, narrates his lyrical memoir about how it feels to set out on the English Channel and save lives, often in the face of anger from anti-migrant protesters.

.

entries.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
entries.summary: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passionNiels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of
entries.content:
Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

This relentless passion attracted to him a large group of young researchers who later became famous in their own right: Wolfgang Pauli, Paul Dirac, Lev Landau, John Wheeler, Max Delbrück, Felix Bloch and many others. Bohr was helped in this by an unusual circumstance that would be worth imitating. His Copenhagen institute, funded by the Carlsberg foundation (the beer people) had labs on the ground floor, and floors of accommodation above it which hosted a cast of collaborators, some staying for days, others years. They all revered Bohr, whose Socratic manner, kindly disposition and seeming lack of ego created a true Republic of Numbers. Carl von Weizsäcker best described the atmosphere as one of “love without limits” for the man.

Bohr’s life story in essence parallels the first half-century of quantum mechanics. Biographies of physicists frequently either stumble on the physics itself, or veer unnecessarily technical. Ball, one of the few people alive today who is equally at home in biology, chemistry and physics, brings decades of explanatory expertise to the task. The amazing discoveries are explained so effortlessly that the reader hardly realises what just happened.

Bohr emerges as someone who greets even half-formed discoveries with enthusiasm, makes sure that credit is given where due, and keeps the momentum going, often exhausting his collaborators with discussions lasting long into the night. His famous intellectual tournament with Einstein at the Solvay Congresses of 1927 and 1930 – probably the greatest in the history of physics – is grippingly recounted (Bohr won in five sets).

Ball doesn’t shrink from the contentious aspects of Bohr’s career, and in fact illuminates them convincingly. The Copenhagen School he headed has sometimes been described as dogmatic and cult-like. Ball argues that this, insofar as it is true, is not to be laid at Bohr’s door. When the physics remained stubbornly opaque, Bohr tried to steer a prudent course between conflicting interpretations. His followers lapsed into dogma only after his death.

Even when he worked at Los Alamos in the 1940s, Bohr did not materially contribute to development of the atom bomb, though his model of the nucleus had started it all. He was in fact very concerned about the consequences of fission weapons, and the book describes his disastrous encounter with Winston Churchill, during which he suggested sharing atomic secrets with the Russians to avert nuclear war. Churchill angrily took this to be nonsense, and treasonous.

Ball also recounts Werner Heisenberg’s famous trip to see Bohr after the Nazi invasion of Denmark in September 1941. Heisenberg, scheduled to give lectures at the German Institute in Copenhagen, was, obtusely, surprised and upset to see that no Danish scientists turned up, despite his long association with and almost filial devotion to Bohr. They subsequently had a guarded conversation about nuclear weapons, each wary of revealing secrets. Ball convincingly argues that Heisenberg’s self-serving rewriting of history after the war, according to which he and other German scientists had done all they could to avoid giving Hitler the bomb, was bunk. All in all, The Man Who Broke Reality reminds us that science is a very human adventure, and that great humans make great things happen.

entries.title: Theodore Zeldin obituary
entries.summary: Revered historian, author and francophile with a novelistic approach to his subjectOn the website the Oxford Muse, which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.”During the French
entries.content:
On the website the Oxford Muse, which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.”

During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. That is also what conversation seeks.”

These reflections were typical of the way in which Zeldin, who has died aged 93, approached the past, transcended academic constraints and hoped for a better human future. “What is missing from the world is a sense of direction, because we are overwhelmed by the conflicts which surround us, as though we are marching through a jungle which never ends,” he wrote in the book Conversation (1998). “I should like some of us to start conversation to dispel that darkness … to create equality, to open ourselves to strangers, and most practically, to remake our working world, so that we are no longer isolated by our jargon or our professional boredom.”

On his 75th birthday, in 2008, Zeldin initiated what he called “a feast of strangers”. Instead of inviting friends to celebrate at his art deco home outside Oxford, he issued an invitation through the media to everybody he did not know, to join him at an art gallery to have a conversation with a stranger. His aim was to get people to really understand one another by encouraging them to talk one-on-one for at least two hours about their priorities and the way they believe life should be conducted.

“I’m constantly astounded by the way people talk so openly to someone they don’t know,” he told an interviewer. “They clarify in their own minds what is important to them, discover another person has similar problems, and create trust and even a friendship.”

At a time when social theorists were inclined to academic obscurantism and/or Spenglerian gloom, Zeldin was an optimist. In An Intimate History of Humanity (1994), he wrote: “It is in the power of everybody, with a little courage, to hold out a hand to someone different, to listen, to attempt to increase, by even a tiny amount, the quantity of kindness and humanity in the world.” Whether one finds that optimism mawkish or inspiring depends on one’s temperament, but his sincerity was undeniable.

Theodore was born to Russian Jewish parents on Mount Carmel, in the pre-Israel British mandate in Palestine. His mother, Emma, was a dentist, and his father, Jacob, was an engineer and mathematician who, Zeldin said in an interview with the Independent, “joined the British colonial service and went round improving the empire”. A child prodigy, he could read by the age of three. His first school report said: “He bestrides the school like a colossus.”

Zeldin wrote his first book aged 12. After attending a boarding school in Cairo, he continued his education at Aylesbury grammar school, Buckinghamshire. At 15, he went to what is now Birkbeck, University of London because, as he said: “It had no upper age limit and thus no lower one either, so I was at university with greyheads.” He graduated with a degree in history in 1951.

He then studied modern history at Christ Church, Oxford, where he had a formative experience. “One of the most silent men I have known ended up committing suicide,” he recalled. Zeldin had been one of a handful of students invited to lunches given by the college’s philosophy tutor. “He brought us together for conversation, but hardly ever spoke himself. And yet there was a wonderful warmth radiating from him, a gentleness, a modesty, which somehow made us talk, shy and ignorant though we were.” One day, there was a note pinned to the tutor’s door warning visitors that he had turned on the gas and they would find him dead.

Thereafter, Zeldin took the task of speaking well as a duty – “like playing music, it requires attention and knowledge and practice,” he observed. He remained in Oxford, first as a DPhil student and later as a fellow of St Antony’s College, where he developed the university’s postgraduate centre for international studies, and was its dean for 13 years.

His home was England, but his passion was France. He wrote The Political System of Napoleon III (1958), co-edited (with Anne Troisier de Diaz) the journals of Napoleon’s prime minister Émile Ollivier (1961) and published a book of essays, Conflicts in French Society: Anticlericalism, Education and Morals in the 19th Century (1970).

But it was his 2,000-page, five-volume History of French Passions (Ambition and Love, Intellect and Pride, Taste and Corruption, Anxiety and Hypocrisy, Politics and Anger), published between 1973 and 1977, that best expressed his idiosyncratic approach to history and earned him enduring adoration. “He understands us better than we know ourselves,” claimed Livres de France. Le Point magazine pronounced him “the most popular Englishman in France”. Policemen saluted him in the street; train conductors upgraded him from second class to first. Zeldin – who was made CBE in 2001 – was appointed to the Légion d’honneur in 2012.

“My method is to hold up a multitude of mirrors around the French, so that they may be seen simultaneously from different angles,” he explained in the preface to Ambition and Love, the first volume. He told a Financial Times interviewer: “In that book I looked at every aspect of life. What does it mean to dance? What does it mean to commit a crime? What does it mean to be anxious? What does it mean to tell a joke? The great thing about the French is that they have thought about these subjects in a great variety of ways and are a very articulate people.”

In 2007, he served on the Attali commission, tasked with suggesting reforms to revivify France to the then president Nicolas Sarkozy. Zeldin’s brief was to come up with ideas to “change mentalities”. Undaunted, he suggested – among other measures – that school teachers be posted to foreign countries for a year to experience different cultures.

His kaleidoscopic, even novelistic approach to history – more Balzacian than Oxonian – served him well in later books, notably An Intimate History of Humanity, in which he interviewed people, mostly French and overwhelmingly female, about human needs and desires, ending up with chapters such as “How men and women have slowly learned to have interesting conversations” and “How people have freed themselves from fear by finding new fears”. He went from personal to epochal, trying to work out how concepts of personal fulfilment, sexual relations or family obligation have differed over time. And he encouraged us to change them again.

He was impressed by those who have imagined how they might change the ends of their lives and then, courageously, cast off the presumed shackles of historical determinism, and thereby realised what they imagined. In his 1988 absurdist novel Happiness, a young woman called Sumdy visits Paradise on a roundtrip ticket and meets kamikaze pilots and Einstein. She returns chastened: happiness, it turns out, is an outdated idea rather than the summum bonum of human life. Such is the novel’s moral and Zeldin’s principal theme: our challenge is to imagine different ends and have the courage to pursue them. Happiness, for Zeldin, was not enough.

In his later years Zeldin’s particular concern was to free people from demeaning work. As an associate fellow of the Saïd Business School in Oxford, and much in demand on the international lecture circuit, he once visited an Indian factory making electrical equipment, where he saw “rows and rows of Indian women fiddling around with bits and pieces”. The manager said he wanted to turn these employees into entrepreneurs. Zeldin replied that it would be impossible if they spent eight hours a day performing boring tasks. The manager agreed to mechanise some of their routine functions and devote two hours a day to educating his workers. “That’s the kind of revolution that interests me,” Zeldin said.

In 1975 he married Deirdre Wilson, whom he met at Oxford when she was an undergraduate and who became emeritus professor of speech, hearing and phonetic sciences at University College London. Wilson became renowned for developing, with the French cognitive scientist Dan Sperber, relevance theory – an attempt to tackle the paradox of how human comprehension can ever be achieved since, as Wilson and Sperber put it in their 2012 book Meaning and Relevance, when people speak, their words never fully encode what they mean, and the context is always compatible with a variety of interpretations.

Doubtless the focus of their research appealed to Zeldin’s sense of the importance of conversation and how, in practice, it works. He said of their marriage: “The fact that we have no children makes it easier for us to separate, but also brings us closer emotionally.” The essence of a relationship, Zeldin believed, is that it must every day seem worthwhile. In that, as in much else, he was an optimist who realised that the art of living requires work as well as virtuosity.

He is survived by Deirdre.

entries.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
entries.summary: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish warNine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dia
entries.content:
Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style.

Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “gjak” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

But the foregrounding of voice, orality and storytelling is equally striking and ever present. Each narrative is framed as a kind of monologue: a breathless speaker delivers an uninterrupted recollection to a seemingly eager, if unresponsive, addressee. In the chapter titled “Do t’a pres koçídhetë” (or “I will cut off your braids”), a suitor tells his potential father-in-law about the vengeance he sought against a comrade who wronged his family. “Fare you well, my dear, I must be gone” takes place at a funeral where garrulous Gousias tells an unnamed interlocutor the deceased’s story of a burgeoning affair deferred by the conflict.

An interesting question that haunts these pages concerns the function of storytelling for these characters. Several problematise or speculate on their impulse to vocalise experience: “Talking to you about it dun’t help,” states one protagonist; “Why am I telling you this anyhow?” wonders another. Is speech, in these instances, an attempt at redemption, understanding or commemoration? Does narration rehumanise these men who had to “unlearn how to be human”? Answers remain teasingly and provocatively elusive.

This talkative tendency acquires an added and ironic layering in the brilliant Knocker, perhaps the most absorbing of the tales. Here the narrator discusses his emigration from Greece to America, where he hoped to find a long-lost figure called Argyris, who had left for the US many years before. After he eventually tracks Argyris down in Chicago, wreathed in cigarette smoke and downing cognac, the two strike up an enigmatic but profound friendship. One notable feature of this bond, which troubles the narrator, is its lack of balance. He is always keen to talk to Argyris about how he is acclimatising to the peculiarities of American life and of his longing for their homeland. Argyris, however, is entirely silent on these matters. Until, one day, he is not. His is a bleak autobiography in which articulating the horrors of war produces unexpected consequences.

Unexpected, too – and testament to the exciting multiplicity of Gjak – is Ballad, in the centre of the collection. Breaking with the conventions of the other stories, as the name suggests, this is a lengthy narrative poem. Here, a “dauntless maiden”, mourning the loss of her beloved, engages in mortal and rhetorical combat with sly Death. Papamarkos and Valvis make skilled use of the traditional ballad form to give the maiden’s lamentations boldness and vitality.

For a work where attention is keenly trained on death, and the threat of death, there is so much boisterous vitality throughout. The immediacy of the idiomatic phrasing, the liberal peppering of expletives and insults, the sensual and homoerotic celebrations of the body even in the midst of slaughter: all this liveliness makes Gjak a defiant statement about a community insistent on its survival.

entries.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
entries.summary: Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthoodBack in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambi
entries.content:
Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place.

Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its sequel, and we’re in metatextual heaven. In the four years of Westish time that have elapsed between the two books, Owen Dunne (baseball player in The Art of Fielding; groom-to-be here) has written and published, to great acclaim, a novel called – guess what! – The Art of Fielding.

It’s a bold move – but Harbach’s gifts as a writer mean that he goes a long way towards pulling it off. The Brightness, which unspools with the same warmth and expansiveness as its predecessor, in the same generous multi-perspective realist mode, folds us in from page one. Returning to Westish after so long away offers the reader the cosiness of a college reunion: the campus, with its “maples and conifers”, its “green geometries of Small Quad and Large”, is pleasurably recognisable, and it’s a treat to check in on old friends. Harbach’s focus shifts away from star shortstop Henry Skrimshander (The Art of Fielding’s least interesting character) on to Owen, and Mike Schwartz, the Harpooners’ former captain, now assistant athletic director. And at the centre of this sequel is Pella: a complex, independent spirit in The Art of Fielding; now, at 27, possessed of all the trappings of secure adulthood, but labouring under a growing sense of restlessness.

But this isn’t purely a nostalgia tour. Alongside the old hands come a new generation of undergraduates, bounding on stage to throw everything into confusion. First among them is Irma Friske, Pella’s closest friend despite the six years between them: a “nerdy and beguiling” scholarship student, possessed of a “finicky mind”. At the novel’s opening, we see Irma turning away from the comfort of her friendship with Pella towards something knottier, but far more electrifying. Together with Pammy Chang and magnetic, troubled Dahlia Breughel, she dreams up a feminist “project” carried out at one of Westish’s notorious start-of-the-semester parties, which culminates in two football players waking up the morning after with a shocking phrase tattooed across their foreheads.

The fallout from the prank (or protest, or art project, or hate crime, depending on your perspective), and the questions it raises about power, consent, and the administration of justice, spreads beyond the campus into the national press. The novel, set in 2015 on the brink of Trump’s first presidency and the global #MeToo movement, captures how such actions might have been seen at the time: as original, as essential, even as a means to celebrity and power. The dramatic irony is that we’re reading about them in the shadow of the recent events at Cornell University – which cast the determination of the girls and their champions in a different light.

Either way the act and its fallout are propulsive: like Henry’s errant throw in The Art of Fielding, they set everything in motion. But here’s where the books diverge: reaction, in The Brightness, only carries things so far. While the first half of the book is tight, focused and plot-driven, the second sees the characters’ expected trajectories petering out. Rather than finding themselves propelled to their destination, they pause, cast around, question the paths they’re on. Where The Art of Fielding was a quest narrative of sorts, The Brightness is closer in form to a picaresque: more nebulous, more provisional; more interested in the journey than the destination.

And this is where its real ambitions lie. If Melville was the presiding genius of The Art of Fielding, in The Brightness Harbach shifts his allegiance to Shakespeare. Macbeth gets a look-in – Irma, Pammy and Dahlia are quickly dubbed “The Witches of Westish” – but the deeper conversation is with The Tempest, Shakespeare’s last solo play and his most magical. Harbach’s young women want to be Prospero, arranging the lives of everyone around them. Irma and Dahlia aren’t content to be characters in someone else’s story: they want to write their own, and to write other people into it. But a story, once loosed on the world, refuses to stay where it’s put. The campus reads it one way; the national press another. Its meaning slips out of their hands.

It is Pella who arrives at the book’s governing insight. “You couldn’t proceed from some shaping wish regarding how things should be,” she reflects, late in the novel. “You couldn’t worry about how your life might look from the outside, to some observer or reader, even if the reader was you.” Or, as another character puts it: “To be in your 20s is to not quite know what the story’s about … You can’t see any shape to it.” The Tempest ends with Prospero breaking his staff and drowning his book. In The Brightness, Harbach steps back from imposing an overarching plot, and lets his characters make their own way, as people in their 20s have to do.

It’s a lovely idea, and a brave one. The trouble is that while shapelessness may be true to life, within a novel, it risks feeling less like freedom than like a story that has lost its way. The Brightness ends on a note of ambiguity – the suggestion that it, too, may be a construct of one of its characters. If that’s the case, we may have to read the next novel to fully perceive this one’s shape and meaning. Let’s just hope we don’t have to wait for another 15 years.

entries.title: The best books to read in November and December: new paperbacks from Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some must-read new paperbacks, from an experimental novel about a German actor to a study of how the arts can boost our health*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

Jesus Christ Kinski

Benjamin Myers

The German actor Klaus Kinski is known best for his testy collaboration with Werner Herzog, whose 1982 film Fitzcarraldo put Kinski in the title role, lugging a steamship over the Andes.

Benjamin Myers’s new novel plunges us into Kinski’s fevered mind during one of his last performances, a recorded solo stage show in West Berlin in 1971, where he delivered a ferocious monologue as Jesus. Showcased in a documentary released in 2008 by Peter Geyer, the act descended into chaos, Kinski arguing with hecklers before ending his monologue in a near-empty auditorium.

The book melds Kinski’s on-the-record words with imagined second-person recollection about, among other things, his capture by allied forces as a German conscript, a spell in a psychiatric clinic, and his innumerable sexual conquests.

Cut half a century later to West Yorkshire during lockdown, where an unnamed writer decides to write a book “about the dead German actor Klaus Kinski”. The project looks unsaleable from the off, not least because Kinski’s eldest daughter, Pola, accused him of sexually abusing her. There’s also the fact that “the writer” – let’s call him Benjamin Myers – owes his publisher a “long, era-spanning historical novel concerning an English saint”, and has already spent the advance (this is a reference to 2023’s Goldsmiths prize-winning Cuddy). Yet the “dark and forceful energy” of Kinski’s Jesus keeps drawing him back to online footage. By the time Myers clocks that the actor was 45 in 1971 – the age Myers is in 2021 – “a psychic door of communication [is] opened by the key of coincidence”, and it would basically be rude not to write the book.

This fitfully engaging narrative experiment isn’t really about Kinski or even Myers so much as the 21st-century cultural marketplace. As lapel-grabbing rants give way to downbeat musings, the book exerts a strange charm, ushering us behind the scenes of its own making. “I live freely,” Kinski boasts, unlike people “stuck in … dismal jobs”. Amid the keynote disaffection, you ultimately sense contentment, even joy, that he’s not the only one able to say so. Anthony Cummins

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The True True Story of Raja the Gullible (and His Mother)

Rabih Alameddine

Meet Raja, the narrator of Rabih Alameddine’s new novel. A 63-year-old gay philosophy teacher and drag entertainer, he is a stickler for rules and boundaries, living in a tiny Beirut flat with his octogenarian mother, the nosy and unfettered Zalfa. Invited to a writing residency in the US, Raja will use the occasion to relate his life.

Winner of the 2025 US National Book Award for fiction, Alameddine’s seventh novel opens and closes in 2023, but the bulk of its action takes place earlier: encompassing the lead-up to and aftermath of the Lebanese civil war (1975-1990), the Covid pandemic, Lebanon’s 2019 banking crisis, and the Beirut port explosion in 2020. If this timeline makes the book sound like a punishing tour of Lebanese history, I promise it isn’t. More than a war chronicle or national exposé, it is a queer coming-of-age tale, an exploration of the bond between a mother and a son, and a meditation on storytelling, memory, survival and what it means to be truly free. Told in a voice as irresistibly buoyant as it is unapologetically camp, this rule-breaking spin on the trauma plot holds on to its cheer in the face of sobering material. Poignant but never cynical, often dark but never dour, wise without being showy and always eager to crack a joke, this is a novel that insists that the pain of the past need overwhelm neither present nor narrative, identity nor personality. With Sartre as his guide, and a drag fabulousness all his own, Raja shows us how. Yagnishsing Dawoor

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Crime and thriller

Crime and thriller

A Bad, Bad Place

Frances Crawford

Set in the late 1970s in the Possilpark district of Glasgow, an area riven by poverty, crime and sectarianism, Crawford’s superb debut is told from two points of view: 12-year-old Janey, who is walking her dog when she stumbles upon the body of a young woman; and her grandmother Maggie, who has cared for Janey since she was rescued, as a baby, from the gas explosion that killed her immediate family. Janey is afraid to tell the police all she knows, but finds herself caught up in the machinations of the grownup world. Maggie, who has secrets of her own, is desperate to protect her granddaughter, but poverty and lack of choice make her vulnerable, and the dead woman has connections to a well-known criminal family. A well-observed, well-told account of trauma, grief and the concomitant magical thinking, this coming-of-age mystery has flashes of humour and pathos that provide fuel for real suspense. Laura Wilson

£8.99 – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Crime and thriller

The Madman

Henning Mankell, translated by George Goulding and Sarah de Senarclens

Written in the 1970s and published in English for the first time, The Madman is set in a Swedish town in the late 1940s. The country’s wartime neutrality-on-paper continues to divide: the town’s pro-Nazis want the past forgotten, but the communist sympathisers, bitter about having been interned, want a reckoning. When a letter to this effect appears in the local paper, those accused, including the director of the town’s sawmill, claim that newcomer Bertil Kras has been stirring resentment for political ends. When the sawmill burns down, Kras is blamed for that, too, and the disintegration of the life he has tried to make provokes an existential crisis. An older Mankell might have been more concise, but the slow build towards inevitable disaster makes for true emotional depth, and the theme of othering, isolating and penalising people for their opinions remains horribly topical. Laura Wilson

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Letters

Letters

John Updike: A Life in Letters



John Updike had the mind of a middling middle-class postwar American male, and the prose style of a literary genius. Such a lord of language was he that even the notoriously grudging Vladimir Nabokov afforded him a meed of praise. A reviewer, musing on the disproportion between the style and content of Updike’s fiction, likened him to a lobster with one hugely overgrown claw. It was a comparison Updike was to remember – for all his bland urbanity, on display from start to finish in this mighty volume of his letters, he could be prickly, and did not take slights lightly.

At the heart of this volume we find the correspondence, from the first half of the 1970s, surrounding Updike’s separation and divorce from Mary, and his affair with and marriage to Martha – the biblical resonances of the names are almost too pat. These pages make for painful reading: Updike could be cruel – to Martha: “Mary’s body (her breasts!) would delight me still, if I could dissociate it from her pinched Unitarian soul …” – but in the main they are either pained, with Mary, or passionate, with Martha. And simultaneously, of course, he was having it off with other loves, old and new.

Are his books read now? Towards the end he made a glum self-assessment: “I have fallen to the status of an elderly duffer whose tales of suburban American sex are hopelessly yawnworthy period pieces.” Perhaps so; but he wrote such prose as to make the envious seraphim sigh. John Banville

£15.29 (RRP £16.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Science

Science

Art Cure

Daisy Fancourt

A professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London, Fancourt researches how social connections and behaviours affect our health. In Art Cure, her first book for a popular audience, she aims to make a scientific case that the arts – from playing music to theatre-going to painting – aren’t a merely aesthetic aspect of life. Instead, they are deeply entwined with our mental and physical wellbeing at every level – from the workings of our cells and molecules to cognition, memory and mood. In an era of shrinking arts funding and overstretched healthcare systems, her message is urgent. But how to compile rigorous evidence for something as holistic, indefinable – and, perhaps, resolutely unscientific – as art?

Fancourt’s answer is to dissect artistic interventions and practices into their component parts. She argues that every arts experience can be broken down into “active ingredients”; could even – if we had the processing power – be converted into binary code. Singing to sick babies becomes a mix of noise buffering, neurological stimulation, human contact and stress reduction. These ingredients trigger biological mechanisms that lead to health outcomes, she explains, and we can test, refine and prescribe them just as we might any cocktail of drugs. With this approach in mind, she surveys the evidence for medical benefits, from wellbeing to brain health, chronic pain and even how long we live.

Art Cure cannot provide answers. But it does make a compelling, compassionate case for broadening how we think about medicine – to encompass people and communities, not just physical bodies, and to recognise that creativity, identity and purpose shape our biology as much as any drug. Jo Marchant

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

History

History

Stay Alive: Berlin 1939-45

Ian Buruma

Berlin had always been a case apart. The legacy of the wild Weimar years – all that artistic and political radicalism, not to mention louche living – had continued under the Third Reich. The city remained defiantly itself and, despite the efforts of high command, mulish about being told what to do. That, at least, had been the situation in 1941.

By the time Ian Buruma’s father, a conscripted labourer from the Netherlands, arrived two years later, Berlin had begun grudgingly to toe the line. The war was going badly now, with the Russians pushing in from the east, and American and British bombs dropping from the skies. Food was scarce, Jewish citizens were being disappeared daily and Hitler and Goebbels, both frequently in the city, were getting more anxious and crueller by the day. Now whenever Berliners met each other in a food queue or a bomb shelter their most likely greeting was Bleiben sie übrig – “Stay alive”.

Nonetheless, argues Buruma, wherever you looked you could still find pockets of resistance. He isn’t referring here to well organised underground networks, but rather to ordinary men and women, not especially brave but still capable of doing the right thing. When Jews were ordered to start wearing identifying insignia, plenty of their fellow Berliners made a point of going up to them in the street and shaking hands. Young Leo Buruma, drafted in to work at a heavy engineering factory, took up with a Ukrainian girlfriend, pointedly ignoring the Nazis’ dictum that, as a “Germanic” Dutchman, he had no business consorting with an “inferior race”.

Other witnesses, such as journalists Ursula von Kardorff and Ruth Andreas-Friedrich, were careful to keep only scrappy and coded memos during the war, but subsequently reconstructed these into coherent narratives for publication. Von Kardorff could never be described as a resister, yet her memoir shows someone trying hard to remain decent in a criminal state. Her father, a successful portrait painter, had lost his teaching job thanks to his opposition to the regime, yet her mother, a textile designer, continued to kit out the homes of the Nazi grandees. Ursula herself delivers warm clothes to Jewish homes but wonders if she is merely doing it to salve her conscience. Her real anguish is reserved for her brother who is fighting for Germany on the eastern front.

None of this is morally coherent and yet, suggests Buruma in this wonderfully nuanced book, it was necessary if you wanted to stay alive, and knew yourself to be neither brave nor craven – but somewhere in the muddled in-between. Kathryn Hughes

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

The Uncool

Cameron Crowe

Crowe previously fictionalised his story in the 2000 film Almost Famous, which he wrote and directed. His lyrical and compulsively readable memoir The Uncool is bookended by the opening of a musical version, which coincides with the death of Crowe’s mother Alice whose aphorisms, including “Put some goodness in the world before it blows up”, are scattered throughout the book.

Crowe’s is a world of aftershow parties filled with characters like Freddie Sessler, a drug dealer who is rumoured to have made his fortune manufacturing pencils; late-night dressing-room jam sessions (Crowe has his guitar gently removed from his hands by a roadie called Red Dog when he attempts to join in with the Allman Brothers); eager, undamaged groupies (he knows a crew called the Flying Garter Girls whose leader Pennie Lane’s credo is “only blowjobs, and that’s it”); and, as the early 70s wear on, omnipresent cocaine use, though Crowe doesn’t partake. “I couldn’t shake the image of my teacher-mother popping up,” he says. “You’re killing brain cells!”

He shadowed Bowie at parties with Ronnie Wood and in the studio with Iggy Pop; he hung out with him day and night in houses he was renting, meaning that he was there to record the heartstopping moment when Bowie suddenly jumped to his feet mid-interview because he thought he’d seen a body fall from the sky.

The Uncool captures an extraordinarily inventive period in which rock music was stretching out in all directions, whether towards country music thanks to artists like Gram Parsons, or the conceptual in albums by the likes of Yes and the Who. Crowe was part of a burgeoning music press that, as well as recommending new bands to its readers, or conveying what rock groups had to say for themselves, would interpret, celebrate and contextualise the huge creative strides some of these musicians were making. Alex Needham

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Joyride

Susan Orlean

Over the course of four decades, seven books and countless exquisite magazine features, especially for the New Yorker, Orlean has profiled celebrities and nobodies, followed cults and choirs, turned her eye to supermarkets and surfers. “Writers fall into two categories: there are those who have something they want to say to the world, and there are those who believe the world has something to tell them,” she observes. Orlean falls squarely into the second camp. There are two kinds of story she likes best: “hiding in plain sight” and “who knew?”.

A memoir is usually neither of these sorts of stories, but Orlean rises to the challenge of writing about her own life with grace. Joyride represents the liner notes to a career of hits. There’s the deliciously “heady, fun, surreal” experience of watching Spike Jonze’s movie Adaptation, based on her book The Orchid Thief, come to life – including being played by Meryl Streep. (Orlean’s account of flipping open Charlie Kaufman’s script for the first time to discover herself in it is laugh-out-loud funny.) A memorable Twitter thread from 2020 – the result of too much rosé on an empty stomach – that made her the “patron saint of pandemic drinking”, gets its moment, too. And harder episodes: a divorce, a cancer diagnosis, the sorrow of moving her mother into a nursing home.

Orlean sees the writing life as one of constant highwire creative reinvention – “you never build equity”, is how she puts it. Her father, who wanted to be writer but became a businessman instead, might have agreed: after she published The Orchid Thief he suggested she consider finally enrolling in law school. Thank goodness she didn’t. “I felt called, I really did, to describe ordinary life in a way that revealed its complexity and poetry – to show how rewarding it is to be open to and curious about the world, and how much joy can be found in letting yourself be surprised.” Mythili Rao

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Essays

Essays

One Aladdin Two Lamps

Jeanette Winterson

In the framing device that opens the Middle Eastern folk tales collected in One Thousand and One Nights, King Shahryar avenges his wife’s infidelity by ordering her execution and marrying a new virgin every night, having each of them beheaded by sunrise so they won’t have time to cheat. When he runs out of victims, the young Persian queen Shahrazad volunteers but stalls her own murder by telling the king one captivating tale after another – and those become the stories we’re reading.

As Jeanette Winterson puts it in her new book – a dizzying whirligig of memoir, history, philosophy, politics and self-help, loosely tied to commentary on the Nights – Shahrazad’s feat of creativity “refuses the present emergency – the contrived drama of a powerful man”. The echo of life in the Trump era is deliberate; for Winterson, the means by which Shahrazad changes her predicament holds out hope for a progressive politics currently losing ground to “radical-rightwing thuggery”. “A better story starts with a better story,” she writes. “Reason will not win the day. Without imagination nothing changes.”

Each chapter opens with a pithy retelling of one of Shahrazad’s tales, spritzed with 21st-century idiom (“The Vizier … has no manosphere where he can vent”), before giving way to wide-ranging reflections on anything and everything, from the history of eugenics, to 13th-century Mali, to the awfulness of the trouser suits “preferred by some CEO types and lots of female politicians”. As opinions on matters big and small fly past, the tone evokes by turns a party political broadcast, Radio 4’s Thought for the Day, an old friend setting the world to rights. Anthony Cummins

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Biography

Biography

The Curious Case of Mike Lynch

Katie Prescott

At least two terrible ironies surround the death of Mike Lynch. One lies in the name of his superyacht, which sank off the coast of Sicily in the early hours of 19 August 2024. He had named the boat Bayesian to honour Bayes’s theorem, a mathematical rule that helps you weigh up the probability of something given the available evidence, which served as Lynch’s guiding light over the course of a tempestuous career. The theorem was “a beautiful key to our minds”, Lynch believed. But it was entirely incapable of predicting the outcome that morning, when the yacht capsized during a storm, killing seven people, including Lynch, his 18-year-old daughter Hannah and his US lawyer, Chris Morvillo.

A second irony lies in the fact that Lynch had just come through the trial of his life, one he felt was bound to end in jail, where he thought he could die. Somehow, to everyone’s astonishment, an American jury had acquitted him and his co-defendant on all 15 counts of fraud.

To celebrate their win, Mike and his wife, Angela, decided to take the Bayesian on a series of cruises around southern Italy, inviting various supporters and associates. Lynch was no sailor, but he loved the seclusion the boat offered, and was immensely proud of its a 72-metre mast, one of the tallest in the world – a feature that some have speculated made it more vulnerable in strong winds, although the yacht’s manufacturer has defended its design. Through July and into August, it pottered around Capri and the Aeolian Islands. Then, in the middle of the month, the court victors were overtaken by a sequence of near-impossible coincidences, as Prescott sets out in pacily written detail. Charlie English

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Politics

Politics

The Mission

Tim Weiner

Why has an organisation with huge amounts of money at its disposal, a record of recruiting the brightest and the best, and the widest of remits, failed to notch up a better record? It’s true that we may not know about many of the CIA’s successes. But we know about a lot of its failures, and some of them have marked US history ineradicably.

In The Mission, Tim Weiner, whose reporting on the CIA in the New York Times was always essential reading, and whose subsequent books on the US intelligence community have a place on the shelves of anyone interested in international affairs, provides a variety of answers to this essential question. As he showed nearly 20 years ago in Legacy of Ashes, his history of the CIA from its founding in 1947 to the end of the 20th century, the agency’s position by the end of the 90s was pretty desperate. It was starved of cash and bleeding talent. A high-flyer who had been station chief in Bucharest was revealed to be working for the Russians, handing them the names of large numbers of agents and employees. But the new US administration that came in at the start of 2001 wasn’t too worried. In March that year, Donald Rumsfeld, the defence secretary, told the joint chiefs of staff: “For the first time in decades, the country faces no strategic challenge.” Six months later came 9/11. The CIA had tried to convince the feckless George W Bush about the looming threat of Islamic ultra-fundamentalism, but no one in the administration listened. The agency was regarded as broken.

Weiner’s sources encompass several senior CIA figures from the period under discussion. These people opened up to him, and as a result the book contains many essential new details. Weiner’s account of Donald Trump’s links to Vladimir Putin in 2016 is clearly based on information from inside the agency, and it leads him to assert openly that Trump was Putin’s polezny idiot – his useful idiot. There are all sorts of other important and fascinating revelations in The Mission. No one has opened up the CIA to us like Weiner has. John Simpson

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop
